definitions.native: are you okay?, is it okay?

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Are you okay right now?

definitions.native: it’s 됐어요, it became, it worked out
definitions.note: Past polite form of 되다. Commonly used to mean “It’s okay / That’s enough / No, thanks” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That’s enough now.

definitions.native: (I told you) it worked out, (you know) it’s done
definitions.note: Casual spoken form of "되었잖아" (past of 되다 + -잖아). Used to remind someone or emphasize something they should already know.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I told you it worked out, so don’t worry now.

definitions.note: Past tense of 되다 with the polite ending -죠, often used to confirm or soften a statement (like “right?” / “you know”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It’s done now, right?

definitions.note: Past tense of 되다 (“to become / to work out”), often used casually to confirm or conclude (like “it became so, right?” or “it worked out, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It's all done now, right?

definitions.native: would it work?, would that be okay?
definitions.note: Often used rhetorically to express doubt or skepticism (like “Do you really think that’ll work?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you really think that will work if you do it like that?

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be okay?
definitions.note: Informal question ending (-니), often used to ask if something will be okay or acceptable.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will it work if we do it like this?

definitions.note: An older/formal ending (-겠소) often used by (usually older) speakers; can express intention or a guess/assumption.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do it like that, it will work.

definitions.native: would that be okay?, will that work?
definitions.note: Polite question form (often used to ask for permission or confirm something is acceptable).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would it be okay if I do it like this?

definitions.native: will be, will work, will do (be okay)
definitions.note: Often used to say something will be possible/okay or will work out; can also express the speaker’s guess.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll have time tomorrow.

definitions.note: Contraction of 되겠지요/되겠지? Often used to guess or assume something (“probably/it should…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This should be okay, right?

definitions.note: Connective form of 되다 with -고 (“and”), used to link to the next clause (often in phrases like ~되고 싶다, “want to become”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to become a teacher.

definitions.note: Often used to acknowledge that something is possible/works, but with a reservation, commonly in the pattern “되긴 되는데 …”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It does work, but it takes a little time.

definitions.native: does it work?, is it possible?
definitions.note: Casual/plain question form of 되다, often used when checking if something will work or be allowed.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Does this work?

definitions.native: does it work?, is it okay?, is it possible?
definitions.note: Polite question form of 되다, used to ask if something is okay/allowed/possible or if something works.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay to take pictures here?

definitions.native: does it work?, is it possible?, is it okay?
definitions.note: Informal/colloquial question form of 되다, often used to ask if something is possible or acceptable.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can I pay by card here?

definitions.native: it works, it goes through, it’s possible
definitions.note: Casual/informal ending -네 often shows the speaker’s realization or mild surprise (like “oh, it works”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Oh, this method works!

definitions.note: Attributive (modifier) form of 되다 used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 방법이 제일 잘 되는 방법이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This method is the one that works best.

definitions.note: Connector ending -는데 added to 되다; often sets background or contrast, like “but/though …”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It works now, but it won’t tomorrow.

definitions.native: does it work?, is it okay?
definitions.note: Question form of 되다 using -니, often used in casual speech.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Does this work?

definitions.note: From 되다 (“to become; to be okay/work”), used with -면 to mean “if/when …”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I have time, I'll call you.

definitions.note: Polite request form of 되다. Very commonly used in set phrases like “좋은 하루 되세요” (= have a nice day).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Have a nice day.

definitions.note: Casual speech. Often used to remind or persuade someone (“See? It works.” / “You can do it.”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: See? If you do it like this, it works.

definitions.native: works, is okay, can do, becomes
definitions.note: Very common polite ending meaning “it works/it’s okay/it can be done,” often used when confirming or agreeing. Can also mean “it becomes/turns into” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It’s okay to meet tomorrow at 10 a.m., right?

definitions.note: Often used in questions or negatives like “되지?” (Is it okay?/Does it work?) or “안 되지” (It won’t work / It’s not allowed).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I do it like this, is it okay?

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 되다, used before a noun to mean “that became” or “that is done/finished.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This is already done.

definitions.native: the one that works, the one that’s done
definitions.note: Informal spoken/written contraction of “된 것” (되다 + 것).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이건 안 되고, 저 된거 써요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This one doesn’t work, so use the one that works.

definitions.native: (someone) says/claims that it will work, (someone) says/claims that it becomes
definitions.note: Quotative form: -다고 attached to the verb. Often used to report what someone said/thought.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friend said it will work tomorrow.

definitions.note: future attributive form of 되다; used before a noun (e.g. ‘될 + N’ = ‘a N that will be/become’)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He is someone who will soon become a doctor.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be okay?, will it become?
definitions.note: A question form of 되다 (“to become / to work out”), often used to wonder or ask if something will happen or be possible.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will this method work?

definitions.native: will it be (okay), would it work
definitions.note: Question form of 되다 used to ask if something is possible or acceptable; often a polite suggestion/confirmation.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would it be okay if I call now?

definitions.native: whether it will, if it will
definitions.note: The ending -(으)ㄹ지 expresses uncertainty or a question like “whether/if …”. Often used with 모르다 (“not know”) or 궁금하다 (“wonder”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't know if things will go well tomorrow.

definitions.native: does it work?, does it become?
definitions.note: Polite formal question form of 되다; used in formal speech (e.g., announcements, customer service).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Does payment work with this card?

definitions.note: Native Korean numeral (used with counters, e.g., 두 개).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Two apples, please.

definitions.note: Connective form of 두다 used to link clauses (often meaning “after leaving/putting …”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I left the door open and went out.
I have a fear of the dark.

definitions.note: Informal/casual form of 두렵다, often used before a following clause (e.g., “두려워서…” = “because I’m afraid…”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 혼자 밤에 걷는 게 두려워요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m afraid to walk alone at night.

definitions.note: Often used with negation, e.g. 두지 마(세요) = “don’t put/leave (it).”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don't put your bag here.

definitions.note: Past modifier form of 두다, used before a noun (e.g., ‘the thing I put/left’).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 책상 위에 둔 휴대폰이 안 보여요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can’t see the phone I left on the desk.

definitions.note: Modifier form of 두다 used before a noun (e.g., 둘 곳 = “a place to put (something)”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There’s nowhere to put this luggage.

definitions.note: native Korean numeral (used before counters; e.g., 둘, 셋, 넷)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Two apples, please.

definitions.note: often used for order in a list or sequence (e.g., first/second/third)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The second one is a little easier.

definitions.native: leave it, put it, keep it
definitions.note: Contraction of 두어. Used after a verb stem to mean doing the action and leaving it that way (e.g., 해 둬 = do it in advance / do it and keep it done).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Leave the door open.

definitions.note: Informal spoken form of 두다 (often used after another verb, as in -아/어 두다 meaning “do and leave it that way / do in advance”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Put it here.

definitions.note: Polite informal (해요체) form of 두다; often used to mean leaving something as it is or putting something somewhere.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Put the bag next to the chair.

definitions.note: often used to mean the space behind something, or the back side of something
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The bag is behind the chair.

definitions.note: used in expressions like “뒤에” to mean later in time or sequence
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Let’s drink coffee after class.

definitions.note: Informal speech. Often implies digging through something to find it.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Rummage through the drawer.

definitions.note: Informal and can sound harsh/threatening depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do that, you’ll seriously die.

definitions.note: command form (informal) of 뒤집다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Flip the pancake.
The bag is on the back side of the chair.
Please go out through the back door.

definitions.note: Used with the informal question ending -나 to ask casually (like “Do you…?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Are you going in now?

definitions.note: Used before a noun to describe it (present-tense modifier form of 들다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There are many people carrying luggage.

definitions.note: From 들다 + connective ending -니: often means “when/after (someone) hears/listens …” and leads to the next clause.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: When I listened to the explanation, I understood.
The exam finally ended.

definitions.note: Commonly refers to a TV series in Korean (like a K-drama), not only the genre "drama."
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These days I’m watching an interesting TV drama.

definitions.note: Commonly refers to a device/tool like a screwdriver, or a driver (software) for hardware.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I installed the printer driver on this computer.

definitions.note: Humble/polite form of 주다, used when the giver (or the speaker’s side) is lower in status than the receiver.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I give a book to the teacher.

definitions.note: Humble/polite form used when offering to do something for the listener (from 드리다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall I carry your bag for you?

definitions.note: Honorific/polite; used to offer to give something to the listener (or someone respected).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall I give you this?

definitions.native: please come in, please step in
definitions.note: Polite request form of 들다 meaning “to enter.” Often used by staff to guide someone into a place.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please come in this way.

definitions.note: honorific polite past form of ‘eat/drink’; used when talking about someone you want to show respect to
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you eat lunch?

definitions.note: Polite/formal honorific question (used when speaking to someone you want to show respect to, e.g., a customer or older person).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would you like to eat now?

definitions.native: will eat, would you like to eat
definitions.note: Polite form (honorific + -(으)시겠어요). Often used to offer or ask politely.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would you like to eat lunch now?

definitions.note: Honorific form used when talking about someone respected; often appears before a noun or in phrases like “드실 거예요.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Grandfather will eat dinner.

definitions.note: Polite question using the honorific form (드시다). Often used when offering food to someone (e.g., a customer or an older person).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would you like to eat dinner?

definitions.note: Used to list options/choices, often in the pattern A든 B든 (“whether A or B”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Whether it’s coffee or tea, it’s fine.

definitions.note: Past modifier form of 들다, used before a noun (e.g., ‘손에 든 책’ = ‘the book (someone is) holding’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The book I'm holding is really interesting.

definitions.note: Connects to the next verb/clause, meaning “and then/and (while) …” (verb stem + -고).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I listen to music and study.

definitions.note: Nominalized form of the verb 듣다 (“to listen/hear”), often used for the “listening” section/practice in language study.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Today I’m going to practice Korean listening.

definitions.note: present attributive form used before a noun (e.g., “a person who is listening”)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There are many people listening to music right now.

definitions.note: Used with the ending -지 (often followed by 않다/못하다/마(요)), e.g. 듣지 마(요) = “don’t listen.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don’t listen to music right now.

definitions.note: This form is the verb stem of 들다, used before endings (for example, 들+고 → 들고).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: ‘들’ is the verb stem of ‘들다’.

definitions.note: Refers to a dog living in the wild (not a pet).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I saw a wild dog in the mountains.

definitions.note: From 들다 (“to hold, lift, carry”); -고 links to the next verb or clause (“and/while”), so 들고 often means “holding/carrying (and then…)”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went home carrying a bag.

definitions.note: From 들리다 (“to be heard; to be audible”). Often used to say something is audible or that you can hear something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can hear the music well from here.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 들리다 (“to be heard”). Used for something being audible or sounding a certain way.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can hear the music well right now.

definitions.note: Plain/informal question ending “-나”. Often used as “들리나?” to check if someone can hear something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you hear my voice?

definitions.note: Polite/honorific form, often used as a question (e.g., on the phone or in a video call).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you hear my voice?

definitions.note: The ending -지 is often used to ask for confirmation (like “..., right?”) or to connect to the next clause.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can hear well, right?

definitions.note: From 들리다 (“to be heard / to sound / to be audible”); it often implies hearing happens naturally (not intentionally listening).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Music can be heard from outside.

definitions.note: Polite/formal question form (-ㅂ니까). Used to ask if something is audible.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you hear my voice?

definitions.note: Informal present form; also used as a casual command meaning “come in.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I come in? Come in.

definitions.note: Often used as an informal command meaning “go in/come in.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Go in first.

definitions.note: From 들어가다; this form is the verb stem + -고, meaning “and” / “then,” used to connect actions or clauses.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went into the room and closed the door.

definitions.note: present modifier form of 들어가다; used before a noun (e.g., “the person who is entering”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: People who are entering must wear a mask.

definitions.native: even if (someone/something) goes in, even if (someone/something) enters
definitions.note: From 들어가다 + -아/어도 (“even if / even though”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I go in now?

definitions.note: Conditional form of 들어가다, used to mean “if/when (someone) goes in/enters.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you go inside, please take off your shoes.

definitions.native: have to go in, need to enter
definitions.note: From 들어가다 (“to go in/enter”) + -아/어야 (“have to/need to”). Often used as “(I/you/we) have to go in.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Now I have to go inside.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 들어가다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m going into the house now.

definitions.note: Past adnominal form of 들어가다; used to describe a noun (e.g., “the person who went in”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I saw the person who went into the room.

definitions.note: Future modifier form of 들어가다; used before a noun (e.g., 들어갈 곳 “a place to enter/go into”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Where is the room I will go into?

definitions.note: Plain imperative form; often used in writing, storytelling, or when speaking down to someone (e.g., a parent to a child).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Come into the room quickly.

definitions.native: please try listening, please take a listen
definitions.note: Polite request form (-(으)세요) of 들어보다, meaning to try doing something (here: listen).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please try listening to this song.

definitions.note: casual (informal) command: “try listening” / “listen and see.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Try listening to this song once.

definitions.note: Polite, casual ending (-아요/-어요). Often used to suggest trying something: “Try listening (to it) / Hear it out.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Try listening to this song once.

definitions.native: have to go in, must enter
definitions.note: Ends with -야, which expresses obligation ("have to / must").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have to go into the classroom now.

definitions.note: polite request/command form often used to invite someone inside
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The door is open, so please come in.

definitions.note: Past modifier form of 들어오다; used before a noun (e.g., ‘the person who came in’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Who is the person who came in earlier?

definitions.note: Informal/plain style; used to tell someone to come inside or to say someone is coming in.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I opened the door, so come in.

definitions.note: Polite informal (요-form). Often used to invite someone to enter.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The door is open. Come in.

definitions.note: Casual past tense with the ending -지, often used to confirm or remind (like “(you) did, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You came into the room earlier, right?

definitions.note: polite present tense of 듣다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I listen to music.

definitions.note: From 들다. Often used for lifting/holding something with your hands (e.g., a bag).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I lift/hold the bag.

definitions.note: Casual way to ask someone to listen or hear you out (often about a problem or request).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will you listen to me for a moment?

definitions.note: Informal past tense question form (often used when speaking to someone younger or in a casual/rhetorical way).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you hear what I said?

definitions.note: Casual/informal question (반말).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you hear what I said?

definitions.note: Past tense of 듣다. Often means “heard” (received a sound or information), and can also mean “listened (to)” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I heard that news yesterday.

definitions.note: Casual/informal past tense of 듣다 (“to hear; to listen”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I heard that story.

definitions.note: informal casual past form of 들다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I picked up my bag.

definitions.note: Past tense, polite style.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I heard that news yesterday.
I carefully picked up the box.

definitions.note: Used with places (e.g., a room, a store).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I stopped by the store for a moment.

definitions.note: Past tense with a confirming/softening ending; often like “(you) heard/listened, right?” or “I heard/listened.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You heard that story, right?

definitions.note: Informal past form of 듣다. Often used when reminding or confirming something (like “you heard it, right?” / “remember?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I heard that news yesterday, you know.

definitions.native: picked up, lifted, held (in one’s hand)
definitions.note: Past tense of 들다 with sentence ending -지, often adds a “you know / right?” nuance.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I picked up the bag, you know.

definitions.note: command/instruction form (informal) of 들여보내다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Open the door and let people in.

definitions.native: you heard (it), you listened (to it), you’ve heard (it)
definitions.note: Honorific + polite style. Often used to confirm information or check agreement (like “you heard, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You heard the announcement just now, right?

definitions.note: Past modifier form of 듣다, used before a noun (e.g., 'the story (I) heard').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The story I heard was really interesting.

definitions.note: often used to describe something that someone is holding or carrying (modifying a following noun)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The flower he’s holding in his hand is pretty.

definitions.note: Future/intentional modifier form of 듣다 used before a noun (e.g., 들을 음악 “music to listen to”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There is a lot of music to listen to.

definitions.note: Casual/informal question meaning “do you want to listen?” or “will you listen?”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you want to listen to this song?

definitions.native: if (someone) gets caught, if (something) is found out
definitions.note: From 들키다: to be caught / to be found out (often about a secret).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If they find out it's a lie, you're in big trouble.
My back hurts.

definitions.note: Often used after a list to mean “etc.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I bought fruit like apples, bananas, etc.

definitions.note: An insult; rude and offensive.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Are you seriously an idiot?

definitions.note: A rude insult; 등신 is slang meaning someone is very foolish.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You idiot, why did you say that?

definitions.note: A loanword commonly used in cafés and restaurants.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I eat dessert after a meal.

definitions.note: Often refers to a car salesperson/dealership representative, or a card dealer in games.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He is a car dealer.

definitions.note: honorific/polite term used when talking about or addressing someone else’s daughter
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Your daughter is at school right now.

definitions.note: Informal/polite style ending (-해). Can describe temperature, weather, or a warm/comfortable feeling.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The weather is warm today.

definitions.note: Often used after a noun to mean “following/according to ~” (like “~에 따라”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Go according to the map.

definitions.note: Command form (casual) of 따라가다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Follow me.

definitions.note: From 따르다 (“to follow”). “-아/어야” expresses necessity (“must/should”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You must follow the rules.

definitions.note: Often describes someone or something that is behind and moving along with you.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The puppy is following me.

definitions.note: Informal casual command form (used with friends, kids, etc.).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Follow me quickly!

definitions.note: Polite informal present form of 따라오다; often used as an instruction/request.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Follow me this way.

definitions.note: Past tense with a casual/polite ending; often implies the speaker assumes or confirms the listener did it.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You followed me all the way here, right?

definitions.note: Often used to mean doing something not together or keeping things not mixed.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sat separately from my friend.

definitions.note: Command form (plain imperative), often used in writing, instructions, or to a subordinate.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Follow me.

definitions.note: In the verb phrase -(으)ㄹ + noun, this is the modifier form meaning “(to) follow / that will follow.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I will follow the rules.

definitions.note: Often used to show the speaker thinks those things are not important or not worth considering.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't need things like that.

definitions.note: Contraction of 따위는. Used to dismiss or belittle something (often translated like “something like that” / “that kind of thing”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't need excuses like that.

definitions.note: Often used to mean something fits or matches perfectly, or a number/time is exact.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 신발이 내 발에 딱 맞아.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These shoes fit my feet exactly.

definitions.note: Shortened colloquial form of "다른"; used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Ask a different person.
My daughter is six years old.
When it rains, the ground gets wet.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t touch this.

definitions.note: Commonly used before 마(라) to make a negative command: 만지지 마(라) = “don’t touch.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don't touch this.

definitions.note: Used after a noun or clause to show degree/amount: “as much as,” “as … as,” or “to the extent that.” Often appears in patterns like “N만큼” or “V-(으)ㄴ/는 만큼.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I speak Korean as well as my friend.

definitions.note: Used before a noun to mean something is worth doing/trying or good enough (often with a verb stem: ~을/ㄹ 만한).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This movie is worth watching.
I often read comics.

definitions.native: there are a lot, is/are many
definitions.note: A casual/exclamatory form of 많다, often used to react or comment (like “wow, that’s a lot”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There are a lot of people.

definitions.native: to be many; to be a lot (numerous/abundant)
definitions.note: Describes that the number or amount of something is large.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This store has a lot of customers.

definitions.note: informal/polite-final ending meaning “is/are many; there’s a lot” (from 많다)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There are really a lot of people.

definitions.native: there are many, there is a lot
definitions.note: Polite present form of 많다. Used for both “many” (countable) and “a lot” (uncountable).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There are a lot of people in this store.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 많다, used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Many people watched that movie.

definitions.note: Used to describe a large amount or high degree; often used with verbs (e.g., eat a lot, study a lot) and can also modify adjectives/adverbs (e.g., much more).

definitions.native: there are many, it’s a lot
definitions.note: Casual/polite ending meaning “(it) is/are …, right?” or used to agree/emphasize.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These days, there’s a lot to do, right?

definitions.note: Often used in conversational speech as part of patterns like “많지 않아요” (not many) or “많지?” (right, there are a lot, huh?).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There aren’t many people.
I want to ride a horse.

definitions.note: Often used when talking about what someone says (e.g., 말을 하다 = to speak).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please speak slowly.

definitions.note: Used after another verb (verb stem + -지 말다) to mean “don’t (do)” or “stop (doing)”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t cry.

definitions.note: Used after a noun/pronoun to mean “not X, but Y.” Often followed by a second noun with “(으)로/로” or just another noun.

definitions.note: Used after a noun (N 말고) to mean “not N; instead/other than N.” Commonly used with “말고는” (= except for).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Not coffee—please give me tea.

definitions.note: Used after a noun to mean “not X but Y” (e.g., X 말고 Y).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Not coffee—tea, please.

definitions.note: Used to mean doing something exactly the way it was said or instructed.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Okay. I’ll do it as you said.

definitions.note: Often used when explaining the meaning of a word or phrase.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you know the meaning of this word?

definitions.note: Used to quote or report a negative command with -라고 (e.g., 말라고 했어요 = ‘(someone) said not to…’).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My mom told me not to eat ramen at night.

definitions.note: Used to strongly repeat a request/command not to do something. Comes from the negative command form of 말다 + 라고요 (quoting/emphasis).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I said, don’t touch it!

definitions.native: I told you not to (do it)
definitions.note: Casual/emphatic: 말라 (don’t do it) + 니까, used to insist or complain that you already said not to.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I told you not to touch it!

definitions.note: honorific word meaning “(someone’s) words/speech”; used especially for what an older person, a superior, or a customer says
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I listened carefully to the teacher’s words.

definitions.note: honorific/polite form of “to say” (used when talking about someone’s words, often a customer/elder)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What was it that you said earlier?

definitions.note: polite/honorific way to say “say/speak”; often used when talking to or about someone you want to show respect to
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please speak slowly.

definitions.note: Informal (casual) command; often used as “~지 말아” (= don’t do ~).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t go out right now.

definitions.note: Usually used after another verb to mean “don’t do it” (e.g., 하지 말아요 = please don’t do it). Polite informal style.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t go out now.

definitions.note: Casual sentence-ending filler used to add emphasis or introduce an explanation (often like “you know” or “I mean”).

definitions.note: Very casual spoken form of 말이다, used as a filler to introduce or emphasize what you’re about to say.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그게 말야, 내가 어제 봤던 영화야.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I mean, that’s the movie I saw yesterday.

definitions.native: it is; I mean; that is
definitions.note: A sentence ending in the 하오체 (semi-formal, old-fashioned) style, from 말이다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My name is Minsu.

definitions.note: “-고” connects verbs, often meaning “and” or “and then.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I said my name and greeted them.

definitions.note: describes a noun (present modifier form of 말하다)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The person speaking over there is my friend.

definitions.note: Informal. Used when recalling what someone said (often from your own experience or something you witnessed).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 아까 선생님이 내일 시험이 있다고 말하더라.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Earlier, the teacher said there would be a test tomorrow.

definitions.native: to say (something), to tell (someone) to say
definitions.note: Quoted command form: “(someone said) to say…” / “(someone told me) to say…”. Often used with verbs like 하다/전하다 (e.g., 말하라고 했어요 = “they told me to say…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Mom told me to say that she’ll be late getting home.

definitions.native: (in order) to say, (in order) to talk
definitions.note: Used to express intention or purpose: “trying/going to say …” or “in order to say …”.

definitions.note: Conditional form of 말하다; often used to mean “if you say (it)” or “if you tell me.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you don’t know, you can say so.

definitions.note: Used when quoting or asking what someone said (e.g., “what did you say?”). Often implies “(you) say…” in context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What did you say?

definitions.note: past attributive form of 말하다, used to describe a following noun (e.g., "the thing/person I said")
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Remember what I said.

definitions.note: plain present tense form of 말하다; often used in writing or formal statements
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He says he’s coming tomorrow.

definitions.note: modifier form of 말하다 used before a noun (e.g., ‘something to say’)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't have time to speak.

definitions.note: casual/informal form (used with friends, kids, or in casual speech)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Tell me honestly.

definitions.native: even if (someone) says, even if (someone) tells
definitions.note: From 말하다 (“to say/tell”) + -아/어도 (“even if/although”). Often used to mean “even if I/you say (it) …” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 내가 말해도 아무도 믿지 않을 거야.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Even if I say it, nobody will believe me.

definitions.note: Imperative form (a command), often strong or used by someone speaking down to another person; can also be used in writing (e.g., instructions).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Tell the truth.

definitions.note: Casual/informal command, often used to ask someone to say something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Tell me what happened.

definitions.note: Expresses obligation/necessity with the ending -아/어야 (often followed by 돼요/해요, but it can appear without it in context).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You have to tell the truth now.

definitions.note: Polite present tense (해요체) of 말하다; used in everyday conversation.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please speak slowly.

definitions.note: Casual/polite sentence ending meaning “(I/you/we) tell (someone), you know / (I/you/we) will tell (someone).” Often used with an implied subject.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll tell you.

definitions.note: Future form of 말해주다, often used before a noun (e.g., “the person I’ll tell”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You’re the person I’ll tell the secret to.

definitions.native: tell me, say it for me
definitions.note: Informal/polite request (해줘 style). Used when asking someone to tell you something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Tell me what happened.

definitions.note: Informal question ending (-나), often used when checking/remembering something (sometimes to oneself).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did I say that?

definitions.note: past tense with a question ending; can be used as a polite question (“Did you say…?”)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What did you say?

definitions.native: did you say (it)?, did you tell (me)?
definitions.note: Past tense + casual question ending (-니), often used with close friends, younger people, or children.

definitions.note: Past tense of 말하다 (“to say; to tell”). In plain written/neutral style, it often appears in narration or reported speech.

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 말하다; used to describe a noun (e.g., “the thing/person I said”).

definitions.note: casual/informal past tense of 말하다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What did you say earlier?

definitions.note: Casual speech. Used to remind someone of something the speaker already said, often like “See? I told you.”

definitions.note: Polite (요-style). Used when reminding someone of something you already said, often with a slightly emphatic or complaining tone.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I told you yesterday too.

definitions.note: Past tense + casual ending; often implies “as I said” or “I told you (so)” in context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I told you so.

definitions.note: Informal/spoken form of 마음.

definitions.note: Casual spelling/pronunciation variant of 엄마, used in speech or texting.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Mom, I'm heading out!

definitions.native: as you want, however you like
definitions.note: Casual/spoken form of 마음대로.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can do it however you want.

definitions.native: oh my goodness, oh my god

definitions.note: Casual/exclamatory ending -네, often used when noticing or realizing something (like “Oh, it’s tasty!”).

definitions.note: Polite present tense (해요체).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This kimchi stew is delicious.

definitions.note: casual (informal) form of 망설이다, used in everyday speech
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I hesitated, so I couldn’t say anything.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you step in for no reason, you'll ruin it.

definitions.note: Used as a swear/curse word to express anger or frustration; can be rude/offensive.

definitions.note: Often used as a curse or insult before a noun (e.g., 망할 놈 ‘damn guy’). Can be rude/vulgar.

definitions.native: and be right, and be correct

definitions.note: Modifier form of 맞다 used before a noun (e.g., “the correct answer”).

definitions.native: is it right?, is it correct?

definitions.note: Polite old-fashioned style (하오체); often used as a short response.

definitions.native: is it correct?, is that right?

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 맞다; also used to agree with someone.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Yes, that's right.

definitions.note: Casual/polite informal past tense of 맞다 (“to be correct”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You were right.

definitions.note: Casual/polite informal past tense of 맞다 (“to be hit”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I got hit by the ball.

definitions.note: Past tense, polite. Often used to confirm someone’s statement ("That’s right").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Yes, that was right.

definitions.native: if (it is) right, if (it is) correct

definitions.native: if (someone) gets hit, if (someone) is struck

definitions.note: Adnominal (modifier) form of 맞다; used before a noun (e.g., 'the right answer').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That is the correct answer.

definitions.note: Used before a noun to mean “that will be correct/right” (the -(으)ㄹ form).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That is the correct answer.

definitions.note: Used before a noun to mean “that will be hit” (the -(으)ㄹ form).

definitions.note: Casual speech. From 맞다 (“to be correct/true”) + -잖아, used to remind someone of something they already know or should agree with (like “you know”).

definitions.note: Used to confirm something (like “Right?” / “That’s right.”); polite style.

definitions.note: Often used to confirm something or ask for agreement (like “right?”).

definitions.note: Often used at the end of a sentence to confirm or agree (like “right?” or “that’s right”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That’s right.

definitions.note: Often used at the end of a sentence to mean “(it’s) right, isn’t it?” or “right?”

definitions.note: Informal (casual) form; used with friends or in casual speech.

definitions.native: to entrust, to leave (in someone’s care)

definitions.note: Often used in casual speech meaning “I’ll do it / I’ll take care of it.”

definitions.note: Used when telling someone to smell something (like a scent).

definitions.note: Modifier form of 맡다 used before a noun (e.g., “the job/task I’m responsible for”).

definitions.native: tie on, fasten, carry (on the shoulder)
definitions.note: From 매다; “매고” is often used to link to the next action (like “and then…”).

definitions.note: Commonly used in Korean for a person who manages a store, team, or department (loanword).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'm the manager of this store.

definitions.note: Often used with the copula (매력적이다) to describe someone or something.

I drink coffee every morning.
I like beer.

definitions.note: Very common in casual speech; similar to “매일” but more colloquial.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I swear, really.

definitions.note: Often used to mean the hair on your head.

definitions.note: Auxiliary use of 버리다 after another verb stem to mean doing it completely or leaving it (often with a nuance of regret or annoyance).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Just forget it.

definitions.note: informal (casual) command form of 버리다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Throw this away.

definitions.note: Often used for habitual behaviors (good or bad).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He has a habit of going to bed late.

definitions.note: This is the -고 form of 버리다, used to link to the next verb (like “and then”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I threw away the trash and went home.

definitions.native: if (someone) throws away, if (someone) gets rid of
definitions.note: From 버리다 + -(으)면 (“if/when”); often used after another verb to mean “end up doing it / do it completely” (e.g., 다 먹어 버리면).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You must not throw away this paper.

definitions.note: A conjugated form of 버리다 used with -지 (often to show contrast or emphasis, or in patterns like -지 마(세요) “don’t …”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t throw this away.

definitions.note: This is the verb stem 버리- with the future modifier ending -ㄹ, used to describe a noun (e.g., “something to throw away”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sort the trash that I’m going to throw away for recycling.
I go to school by bus.
I spread butter on bread and ate it.

definitions.note: Casual/informal form (e.g., to a friend).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Hold on a little longer.

definitions.note: This is the verb stem form of 버티다, used before endings (e.g., 버틸 수 있어요).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can hold out a little longer.

definitions.note: Used as a counter for how many times something happens.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 그 영화를 두 번 봤어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I watched that movie twice.

definitions.note: Used to label or identify something by number (e.g., in a list, order, or contest).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m number 3.
Lightning struck in the sky.

definitions.note: Attached to a number to make an ordinal (e.g., 첫 번째 = first, 두 번째 = second).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 오늘은 한국에 온 지 세 번째 날이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Today is my third day since coming to Korea.

definitions.note: Often used for phone numbers, ticket/order numbers, and assigned numbers (e.g., student number).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What’s your phone number?
A bee is sitting on a flower.

definitions.note: Often used in phrases like 벌을 받다 (to receive punishment) or 벌금을 내다 (to pay a fine).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you break the rules, you get punished.

definitions.note: Commonly used for small creepy-crawlies in general; can be a bit gross/negative depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: A bug came into the room.

definitions.note: Informal style; often used as a command (“spread/open it”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Spread your legs a bit.

definitions.note: Often used to show surprise that something happened earlier than expected (like “already?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Are you already home?

definitions.note: From 벌어지다; often used for events or situations that occur (sometimes unexpectedly).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What is happening?
The police caught the culprit.
If you commit a crime, you get punished.
That man is a criminal.
There are many laws in Korea.

definitions.note: Common in everyday phrases like "이 방법" (this method) or "그 방법" (that method).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please tell me how to do it.
The defendant heard the verdict in court.

definitions.note: informal command form ("take it off/peel it off!")
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Take off your shoes!

definitions.note: This is the verb stem form used before endings (e.g., 벗어 주세요).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please take off your shoes.

definitions.note: Often considered offensive when referring to a person; use 말 못하는 사람 or 벙어리장갑 (for the gloves) in many everyday contexts.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He was mute from birth.
There is a big wall in this room.

definitions.note: Often used for making an excuse to avoid blame or responsibility.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That's just an excuse.

definitions.note: Commonly used as an insult meaning someone with abnormal or creepy sexual behavior.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That person seems like a pervert.

definitions.note: Used in biology (e.g., insects changing form).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Butterflies become adults through metamorphosis.
I'll contact my lawyer first.
There are so many stars in the night sky.

definitions.note: Often used with negation (e.g., 별거 아니야) to mean “it’s nothing special / it’s no big deal.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That’s nothing special.

definitions.note: Often used with negative expressions like 안/못 or 아니다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't really like coffee.
My friends call me by my nickname.

definitions.note: Often used in questions like “별일 있어요?” meaning “Is anything going on?”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Has anything unusual been going on lately?

definitions.note: Often means a (glass/plastic) bottle or a bottle-shaped container.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please give me one bottle of water.
I caught a cold, so I went to the hospital.
That country doesn’t have enough troops.

definitions.note: Used in healthcare contexts to mean a patient’s past illnesses and treatments.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: At the first visit, they ask in detail about your medical history.
He served in the army as a soldier.

definitions.note: This meaning is mostly used in formal contexts (often written as 病死).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 배우는 병사로 세상을 떠났다고 전해졌어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It was reported that the actor passed away from illness.

definitions.note: Plural of 병사 (“soldier”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The soldiers marched along the road.

definitions.note: Very offensive Korean insult (ableist slur). Avoid using it; it’s used to harshly demean someone.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You shouldn't call other people an idiot.
My mother is at the hospital.

definitions.note: Informal imperative ending often used by older speakers (especially men) to someone younger or of lower status.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Take a look at this.

definitions.note: Informal question form of the auxiliary 보다 (“to try” after a verb). Often used as a suggestion/challenge.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will you try doing this too, just once?

definitions.note: Connective form of 보다 used to link actions ("do X and then do Y").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I watched a movie and then went home.

definitions.note: -고도 is a connective ending meaning “even though; despite.” It links to the next clause.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Even though I saw it, I pretended not to know.

definitions.native: to see, to watch, to look
definitions.note: This is the verb stem of 보다 (“to see”). It’s used before endings (e.g., 보기만 해도 = “just by looking”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Just seeing it makes me laugh.

definitions.note: From 보다 + -기는. Often used to show contrast or concession, like “I did see/watch it, but …” (as in “보긴 봤지만 …”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 영화는 보긴 봤지만 내용이 기억 안 나요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I did watch the movie, but I don’t remember the story.

definitions.note: Informal/short form used in casual speech; often said as a command (“Send it.”) or in informal endings.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Send the email now.

definitions.note: “-고” connects to the next clause and means “and/then.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sent a message and went home.

definitions.note: Attributive (modifier) form of 보내다; used before a noun (e.g., “the person sending...”, “the message I’m sending...”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please check the email I’m sending.

definitions.native: please send, please give (to someone), please let (someone) go
definitions.note: Polite command/request form of 보내다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please send the photos to this email address.

definitions.note: From 보내주다; often implies doing it for someone (a favor) because of -주다.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 내일 이 서류를 보내줄 사람을 찾고 있어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'm looking for someone who will send these documents tomorrow.

definitions.native: send it (for me), let me send it
definitions.note: Informal request form of 보내주다; often means doing the sending as a favor.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Send me this file by email.

definitions.note: past attributive form of 보내다, used to modify a noun
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you get the email I sent?

definitions.note: Future/intent form of 보내다, used before a noun (e.g. 보낼 편지 = “a letter (I) will send”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll write the email I’m going to send tomorrow now.

definitions.note: casual/informal past tense of 보내다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sent a message to my friend yesterday.

definitions.note: Polite past tense of 보내다 (“to send”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sent a message to a friend.

definitions.note: Question form of 보다; can sound casual or confrontational depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What are you looking at?

definitions.note: Present (adnominal) form of 보다, used before a noun (e.g., ‘the person who is watching’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Who is the person watching TV right now?

definitions.note: From 보다 + -는데. Often links to the next clause meaning “while/as (someone) watches/sees…” or setting up background/contrast.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I was watching a movie when I got a call.

definitions.native: when I saw, when I looked (and then realized)
definitions.note: From 보다 (“to see”). Used to mean “when/as I look(ed), I find/realize that…”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: When I looked out the window, it was snowing.

definitions.note: used to compare two things; placed after the thing being compared (A보다 B = B than A)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I like tea more than coffee.

definitions.note: A quoted command form of 보다 (“to see/look/watch”), often used in indirect commands like “(someone) told (someone) to look.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The teacher told us to look at the book.

definitions.note: Informal, emphatic command (from 보라 + -고), often like “I’m telling you to look!”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Look here, I’m telling you!

definitions.note: Used after a verb stem + -러/-(으)러 to mean “in order to… (go/come)”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to the movie theater to see a movie.

definitions.note: From 보다 (“to see”) + -(으)면 (“if/when”). Often used to mean “if you look” or “when you watch.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: When I see this photo, I smile.
This box is a very old treasure.

definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 반지에는 작은 보석이 박혀 있어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This ring has a small gemstone set in it.

definitions.note: Polite request/command form (often used to tell someone to look at something).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please take a look at this.

definitions.note: polite request/command form (often used like “please” + verb)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please look at this photo.

definitions.note: honorific + polite question form (asking respectfully)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you see that movie?

definitions.note: Polite past form of 보다. Often used as a polite question meaning “Did you see/watch...?”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you see that movie?

definitions.note: Honorific + past tense, with "죠" meaning something like "right?" / "you know" (seeking agreement).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You watched that movie yesterday, right?

definitions.note: A loanword used in everyday speech (e.g., at work or as “the boss” in a game).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Our boss was late to the meeting today.

definitions.note: Honorific past adnominal form of 보다, used before a noun or in phrases like “보신 적 있다” (“have (ever) seen”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It’s a movie that my grandfather watched.

definitions.native: do you see?, would you like to see?
definitions.note: Very polite (formal) question form of 보다; often used as a respectful question to the listener.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you see over there?

definitions.note: past tense of 보다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I saw that movie yesterday.

definitions.note: Informal speech style; often used as the present form of 보이다 (“to be seen/visible”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can see the mountain from here.

definitions.note: Informal (casual) present form of 보이다; often used to describe how something appears.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These clothes look pretty.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 보이다; often used to say something seems a certain way (e.g., “It looks good”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This looks really delicious.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 보이다; can mean something is visible (or “I can see it,” depending on context).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can see the mountain over there well.

definitions.note: future modifier form used before a noun (e.g., ‘the thing/person I will show’)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have photos I will show you tomorrow.

definitions.native: shall I show you?, want me to show you?
definitions.note: A casual way to offer to show someone something. Often implies “for you.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Want me to show you the photo?

definitions.note: casual/informal request (to a friend or someone younger)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Show me the photo, please.

definitions.note: past tense, informal polite (해요체) speech level
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That movie looked really fun.

definitions.note: Used to contrast with the next clause, similar to “although it looks/seems…”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Although it looks small, it’s strong.

definitions.native: can you see it?, do you see it?
definitions.note: Casual/informal question form, often used with friends or in a challenging/teasing tone depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you see it well from there, too?

definitions.note: Casual sentence ending; often used when you notice or realize something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can see the mountain over there.

definitions.note: Attributive (adnominal) form of 보이다, used to describe a noun (e.g., 'a visible thing').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That building you can see over there is our school.

definitions.native: it looks like; it seems (to me) (that…)
definitions.note: From 보이다 (“to be seen; to look”) + -는데. Used to express the speaker’s observation/guess (“it looks/seems…”) and often to gently lead into a suggestion, question, or contrast.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 밖에 비가 오는 것처럼 보이는데, 우산 가져갈까요?
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It looks like it’s raining outside—should we take an umbrella?

definitions.native: it looks like…, it seems…, I can see…
definitions.note: Form of 보이다 (“to be seen; to look/seem”) + polite ending -는데요, which softens the statement and often invites a response or implies “you know…” / “but…”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It looks like it’s raining outside.

definitions.native: do you see (it)?, can you see (it)?
definitions.note: Casual/informal question form of 보이다 (“to be seen, to look/appear”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you see it well?

definitions.native: can you see it?, is it visible?, do you see it?
definitions.note: Polite form; often used to ask if something is visible or to draw attention (e.g., “Do you see?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you see the letters here?

definitions.native: do you see (it), can you see (it)
definitions.note: honorific + formal question (spoken politely to the listener)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you see that mountain over there?

definitions.native: you can see (it), it looks (like), it appears
definitions.note: Polite ending often used to confirm something or check if someone sees it (similar to “right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can see the mountain over there, right?

definitions.note: Casual speech form often used to say something appears a certain way (e.g., ‘보이지?’ = ‘You see?/Right?’).

definitions.note: Often used to mean something “looks/seems” a certain way (to the speaker).

definitions.native: that (it) looks, that (it) can be seen
definitions.note: Quotative/reported-speech form of 보이다, used when saying what someone says/thinks about how something looks or whether it is visible.

definitions.note: Future/intent form of 보이다 (“to be seen; to show”).

definitions.note: Used after a verb stem with -아/어 to suggest trying something together (e.g., 해 보자).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Let's try eating it.

definitions.note: Used to suggest doing something together; from 보다 (“to see/look/watch”). Often used to mean “let’s see (what happens/what it is).”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Let’s see.

definitions.note: Often used when suggesting doing something together (e.g., meeting or watching something), as in “(someone) said, ‘let’s see/watch…’.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I said, “Let’s watch a movie tomorrow.”

definitions.note: Auxiliary form of 보다 used after another verb (often with -아/어) to mean “try doing” or “do and see,” as in 해 보지 (“you should try it”).

definitions.note: This is 보다 + -지, commonly used before 말다 to mean “don’t (do)” (e.g., 보지 마 = “don’t look”).

definitions.note: Commonly refers to a small boat; a loanword from English.

definitions.note: Commonly used for a parent or legal guardian (e.g., at schools, hospitals).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Minors need a guardian’s consent.

definitions.note: Often used in set phrases like "행복" (happiness) or "복 받다" (to receive good fortune).

definitions.note: Usually means a person who does boxing (the sport). It can also mean “boxer shorts,” but that meaning is less common without context.

definitions.note: Used in grammar/linguistics (opposite of singular).

definitions.note: Polite informal style; also used for places/situations meaning “crowded/busy.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This problem is a bit complicated.

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 보다, used before a noun (e.g., “a movie (I) have seen”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The movie I saw was really fun.

definitions.note: Often used when someone has a stage name or nickname.

Our company’s headquarters are in Seoul.

definitions.note: Often used in formal contexts (forms, announcements, customer service) to refer politely to the person themselves.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 본인 확인을 위해 신분증을 보여 주세요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: To confirm your identity, please show your ID.

definitions.note: Used in the pattern -아/어 볼 to mean “try doing (something)” or “give it a try.”

definitions.note: Future attributive form of 보다 used before a noun (e.g., 볼 영화 = “a movie to watch”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I chose a movie to watch tonight.

definitions.native: shall we try..., should we try...?
definitions.note: Used after a verb to suggest trying something (from the auxiliary 보다 “to try”). Often used when making a casual suggestion to yourself or someone else.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall we try eating it?

definitions.native: shall I/we see?, should I/we take a look?
definitions.note: A casual question form of 보다, used when suggesting or wondering what to do (“Shall we…?” / “Should I…?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall we watch a movie?

definitions.note: Used to make a gentle suggestion or invitation ("Shall we...?"). Also used to softly ask "Should I/we try...?"
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall we watch a movie?

definitions.native: shall we look?, should we see?
definitions.note: A polite suggestion/question form meaning “shall we/should we…?”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall we look at the menu now?

definitions.native: want to (do), would you like to (do)

definitions.note: Contraction of 보다 + -(으)ㄹ래, used to express the speaker’s intention or to ask/suggest something in an informal way.

definitions.native: want to (do), would you like to (do)
definitions.note: Used after a verb stem to suggest or ask about doing something together (e.g., 가 볼래요? “Do you want to go?”).

definitions.native: want to see, would you like to see
definitions.note: Polite. Used to suggest or ask about doing something (from 보다, “to see/watch”).

definitions.note: A polite suggestion form ("let's ...") from 보다; often used to propose doing something together or to check/try something.

definitions.note: Auxiliary form of 보다 used after a verb (often with -아/어) to mean “try doing” something or “see what happens.”

definitions.note: Informal speech form of 보다; also used as a casual command meaning “look/see.”

definitions.native: even if (someone) sees, even if (someone) watches/looks

definitions.note: informal/casual; often used to get someone’s attention or to tell them to check something
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Look at this.

definitions.note: From 보다 + -아/어야, used to mean “have to/should (do)” or “only if/after (doing)”.

definitions.note: Casual spoken form of "봐야 하지"; often used to say you’ve decided you should/need to look or check something.

definitions.note: Polite form used as an auxiliary after a verb (-(아/어) 봐요) to mean ‘try doing it’ or ‘see what happens.’

definitions.native: will you do me a favor and…?, can you… for me?

definitions.note: Polite question form of 보다 (“to see”).

definitions.native: did you see?, did you watch?

definitions.note: Past tense of 보다 (“to see/watch/look”), followed by -는데, which often sets background or contrast (“but/and/as for…”).

definitions.note: casual/informal question form (often used to ask someone close to you)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you see that movie?

definitions.note: past tense, plain/informal style (often used in narration or casual speech)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I watched that movie yesterday.

definitions.native: (someone) said they saw (it), (someone) said they watched (it)
